extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of literary theory and creative writers studying narrative technique
extracted.subtask_description: Summarize and apply Wayne C. Booth's theoretical criteria for analyzing and producing fiction, emphasizing authorial presence, narratorial reliability, showing/telling choices, distance, and the ethical effects of literature (coduction). Useful for critiquing novels and teaching narrative craft.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authorial presence and judgement (real or implied author)
rubrics_metrics.description: Booth's defence of the author (either 'real' or 'implied') as an interplay of judgements and observations that give 'ironic complexity', 'intensity of illusion', 'portrayal of moral ambiguities', 'revelation of truth' and 'prophetic vision'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat every textual choice as a sign of authorial judgement: 'though the author can to some extent choose his disguises, he can never choose to disappear'. Evaluate how authorial stance, explicit or implied, shapes interpretation, ethical orientation, and the reader's responses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Showing vs telling (deconstruction of the binary)
rubrics_metrics.description: Booth problematises the conventional aesthetic hierarchy that prizes 'showing' over 'telling', arguing that all showing reveals interpretive choice and that sometimes 'telling' can be more successful and interesting than showing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing narrative technique, don't assume 'show, don't tell' is absolute. Examine whether 'showing' or 'telling' better serves the text's judgments and effects (e.g., compressing time by saying 'ten years went by' versus describing changes). Consider the interpretive choices and critical judgement implicit in either mode.

rubrics_metrics.name: Narratorial reliability (reliable vs unreliable narrator)
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinguish between relatively trustworthy narrators and those 'economical with the truth'. Unreliability may be deliberate or caused by restricted vision, ideological intensity, or mental incapacity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate narrators for signs of deliberate deception or limitations (restricted perspective, ideology, psychological instability). Use examples like the Governess in Henry James's The Turn of the Screw and Atwood's Surfacing to analyse how unreliability produces ambiguity of effect and shapes reader inference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Confusions of distance (causes that problematize narrative distance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Booth lists causes that complicate the reader's sense of distance from the narrator/text: 'lack of adequate warning that irony is at work'; 'extreme complexity, subtlety, or privacy of the norms to be inferred'; and 'vivid psychological realism'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the text signals irony adequately, whether the norms it expects readers to infer are excessively private or subtle, and whether powerful psychological realism blurs critical judgement. These factors can create 'unintentional ambiguity of effect' and sympathetic responses to morally dubious protagonists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Degree of interiority/stream-of-consciousness and its effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Booth warns that 'deep plunges' into interior consciousness (streams-of-consciousness, autobiography) can 'bind the reader so tightly to the consciousness' that it blinds them to the possibility of making judgments not shared by the narrator.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating interior techniques, consider whether intense subjectivity prevents readers from making independent judgements or whether it is deliberately used to create ambiguity. Judge the ethical and interpretive consequences of binding readers to a character's consciousness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement for textual factual bases to ground judgments
rubrics_metrics.description: Booth resists relativism by insisting that 'certain “factual” bases must exist in a text for judgments to be grounded', enabling critics to avoid infinite co-present interpretations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether a reading is supported by textual facts and evidence rather than purely speculative or relativistic claims. Check that interpretive claims have anchoring details in language, events, or narrative structure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ethics of fiction and coduction (values embedded in texts)
rubrics_metrics.description: Booth's concept of 'coduction' describes a process of evaluation and ongoing conversation based upon previous experience of texts; he argues that texts contain 'a set of values' that affect and can transform the reader's value system.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyse the ethical implications of a work: what values does the text embody or promote, how does it invite readers into a conversational evaluation with prior texts, and what moral effects might result from encountering the Other in the narrative? Consider coduction as both an analytic and pedagogic tool.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reader-response interaction vs embedded textual values
rubrics_metrics.description: While engaging with Reader Response Theory, Booth holds that coduction implies values embedded in a text 'regardless of the need for a reader to respond to them'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balance attention to readers' responses with close analysis of the values and judgments encoded in the text itself. Evaluate both how readers might respond and what the text itself asserts or implies ethically and rhetorically.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pedagogic and rhetorical dimensions (teaching, clarity, and the impact of literature)
rubrics_metrics.description: Booth's work has pedagogic aims and concerns with teaching, rhetoric, and the impact of literature (e.g., his presidency of MLA and founding of Critical Inquiry reflect this orientation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When using Booth's framework for assessment, consider didactic clarity and the work's capacity to teach, provoke ethical reflection, or shape critical skills. Judge whether a text is effective as an object of instruction and rhetorical formation.
